nameStory: The Swimming Anemone gets its remarkable name from its unique ability to literally swim away from danger - something almost no other sea anemone can do! While most anemones stay firmly planted in one spot like underwater flowers, this little marvel can detach from its base and propel itself through the water with rhythmic contractions when threatened by predators.
description: The Swimming Anemone is a small, colorful sea anemone that looks like a living underwater flower with tentacles instead of petals. Its body comes in warm shades of reddish-orange to brownish colors, making it stand out against rocky surfaces. Like other anemones, it has a cylindrical body topped with a crown of soft, waving tentacles that it uses to catch tiny prey floating by. What makes this species truly special is its ability to swim - a superpower almost no other anemone possesses.

idTips.label: Swimming Ability
idTips.description: Can detach from surface and swim with rhythmic, pulsing motions when disturbed - watch for this distinctive escape behavior that separates it from all other local anemones

idTips.label: Color Pattern
idTips.description: Body displays warm reddish, orange, or brownish tones that feel vibrant against the cool ocean colors - often with subtle variations in intensity

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small and compact compared to other anemones, fitting easily in the palm of your hand when fully extended

idTips.label: Tentacles
idTips.description: Crown of soft, flexible tentacles that feel slightly sticky to gentle touch and wave gracefully in the current

idTips.label: Body Texture
idTips.description: Smooth, somewhat rubbery body wall that feels firm but yielding, like a water balloon filled with gel

habitat: Look for Swimming Anemones in cold New England waters, typically attached to rocky surfaces, shells, or other hard substrates in subtidal zones. They prefer deeper waters where divers and snorkelers might encounter them, often in areas with good water circulation that brings plenty of food particles.

seasonality.spring: Active in cold spring waters as marine life becomes more active. Best time for diving observations as water begins to warm slightly.
seasonality.summer: Most easily observed during summer diving season when water visibility is typically at its best and the anemones are actively feeding.
seasonality.fall: Still active in early fall, though diving conditions may become more challenging as water temperatures drop and storms increase.
seasonality.winter: Present but rarely observed due to harsh winter diving conditions in New England waters, though they remain active in the cold depths.

funFact: When a Swimming Anemone detects the scent of certain predatory sea stars, it can literally launch itself off the seafloor and swim away by rapidly bending its body back and forth - imagine a flower suddenly coming to life and doing backflips through the water to escape danger!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small, colorful anemones like the Frilled Anemone, but the Swimming Anemone's escape-artist abilities are a dead giveaway - if you see an anemone swimming away from you, you've found your species! Remember: most anemones are homebodies, but this one has places to go.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'Swimming' Anemone, it only swims when absolutely necessary as an escape mechanism - it's not constantly swimming around like a jellyfish. The rest of the time it lives attached to surfaces just like its more sedentary cousins, making this behavior all the more remarkable when witnessed.
compareHints: As the only Stomphia species documented in New England waters, the Swimming Anemone is unique in its family for its escape-swimming behavior. Other anemones in the Actinostolidae family are strictly bottom-dwelling and cannot swim, making this species' mobility its most distinguishing family trait. When comparing to other small, colorful anemones in New England, always test for the swimming response - it's the ultimate field mark.
